newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak brokers call for independent market watchdog.
newsitem.headline: Slovak brokers call for independent market watchdog.

text.p: Slovak stockbrokers on Thursday called for the creation of an independent control body modelled after the U.S. Securities and Exchange (SEC) to try to boost the market's sagging image.

Valer Ostrovsky, chairman of the Association of Securities' Traders (AOCP), told Reuters the body should be an effective legal authority with executive powers and that it should also be fully independent from any state influence.

"An independent control body would really help improve the enviroment on the capital markets.... but we mean independent and not influenced by state authorities," Ostrovsky said at an AOCP general assembly in Bratislava.
At present, the only supervisory body covering the capital markets is a special oversight section of the finance ministry.
Investors and analysts have repeatedly criticised state supervision of the market, saying it has been uneven and ineffective.
Several international economic institutions, including the World Bank, have also recommended the creation of an independent capital market watchdog.

In a recent a report the bank said much of the market's regulation was left to the administrative discretion of the ministry of finance and had no transparent standards or criteria for decision-making.
One broker told Reuters that the creation of an independent supervisory body was unlikely in the foreseeable future, however, since official authorities appear satisfied with the current situation.
"There seems to be lack of political will to take control over the capital markets from the competence of the finance ministry," the broker, who did not wish to be named, said.

The Bratislava Strock Exchange (BSE) is one the smallest to emerge from post-Communist Europe with market capitalisation of $2.6 billion, compared with the region's largest, Prague, which has capitalisation of some $16 billion.

The Slovak market has long been plagued with low liquidity and little investor interest due to uncertanity over the country's future political orientation, a murky privatisation process and a perceived hostile attitude to foreign investors.

In addition to a market watchdog, brokers said the market desperately needed more issues since the majority of shares traded on the BSE are of companies privatised through vouchers, most of which have a majority shareholder.
Local companies very rarely turn to the capital market to obtain funds for investment projects.
"The scrapping of the second wave of voucher privatisation and replacing it with (a) bond scheme have damaged the market's image among the so called local middle-class investors," Ostrovsky said.
He added that such a group of investors was also vital for the inflow of more large foreign institutional investors.
